query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: For refractory metals used as fusion plasma-facing components, the upper-temperature limit of usable plastic strain and impact toughness is primarily governed by oxygen-induced loss of grain-boundary (GB) cohesion; suppressing GB oxygen segregation (e.g. by adding strong oxygen scavengers that bind O in intragranular nano-oxides) will at a given grain size at least double uniform tensile elongation and increase room-temperature Charpy absorbed energy by ≥50 % after identical heat treatments and thermomechanical histories.
generation.material_initial_state: Recrystallised, 99.9 % purity tungsten with equiaxed 1–10 µm grains, ≤5 appm bulk oxygen, no deliberate alloying additions, vacuum-annealed at 1200 °C/2 h.
generation.intervention: Add 0.5 at.% Ti (or Zr) and consolidate under identical conditions so that >80 % of the O is trapped as intra-granular TiO (or ZrO₂) nanoparticles; all other processing parameters held constant.
generation.conditions: Unirradiated specimens tested in vacuum or inert gas at 800 °C in uniaxial tension (strain-rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹) and at 25 °C in instrumented Charpy impact; hydrogen/helium content <0.1 appm; grain size matched within ±10 %.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary oxygen areal density (monolayers of O).
generation.mechanism: O atoms segregate to GBs, reduce the cohesive energy and suppress dislocation emission/absorption. This promotes intergranular micro-cracking and early strain localisation. Scavenger elements form stable intra-granular oxides that lower GB O coverage, restoring GB cohesion and enabling sustained dislocation glide across boundaries, thereby increasing high-T ductility and fracture toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, the Ti-doped alloy will show (i) ≥100 % increase in uniform plastic strain (e.g. 2 % → ≥4 %) at 800 °C, (ii) ≥50 % higher total elongation, (iii) ≥50 % higher Charpy V-notch energy at 25 °C, and (iv) TEM/APT will reveal ≥3× lower GB O concentration (<0.1 monolayers) with no increase in GB cavity density.
generation.baseline: Undoped, nominally high-purity tungsten tested identically.
generation.boundary: Valid for 600–1000 °C, grain size 1–10 µm, total O ≤0.1 wt %, O‐getter additions 0–1 at.%, and in the absence of significant He/H irradiation damage; outside this range other mechanisms (e.g. grain-boundary sliding or He bubble formation) may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative effect size is extrapolated from limited impurity embrittlement studies; magnitude may vary with exact O level and nanoparticle size distribution. Competing segregation of C, N or P could confound results.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare matched pairs of tungsten mini-tensile and Charpy specimens with and without 0.5 at.% Ti under identical powder metallurgy and HIP conditions; measure GB O concentration by atom probe tomography, perform 800 °C tensile tests and room-temperature instrumented Charpy tests.
measurements: GB O areal density (atoms nm⁻²) via APT
Fractography to quantify intergranular vs transgranular fracture
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If GB O density in Ti-doped material is reduced by >50 % yet uniform elongation increases by <20 % and Charpy energy by <25 %, or if fracture mode remains predominantly intergranular, the hypothesis is falsified.
